In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no significant difference in the efficacy of a therapeutic management programme for type 2 diabetic patients that includes SMBG compared with a similar programme that does not include SMBG.
the use of SMBG in the management of type 2 diabetic patients treated with oral antidiabetic drugs is not supported by evidence from randomized controlled trials.
there is insufficient evidence to recommend the routine use of SMBG in patients treated with a glibenclamide‐based regimen.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the addition of SMBG to a therapeutic management programme for type 2 diabetics does not improve HbA1c levels.
the use of self-monitoring of blood glucose is not recommended in patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes who are treated with diet alone or diet and oral antidiabetes drugs.
the addition of self monitoring of blood glucose to usual care in patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes is beneficial for the majority of patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the benefits of using a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) are not limited to people with type 1 diabetes.
the use of a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) in patients with type 1 diabetes is associated with a significant reduction in the rate of severe hypoglycemia.
SMBG is not a panacea for diabetes management, and it is important to understand the context of SMBG and its limitations.
